title: Forms of Address
short: Use titles such as Mr., Ms., Mrs., Mx. or Dr. with a last name until invited to use a first name, and use the name and title a person prefers.
trouble: Learners use "Mrs." for any married-looking woman or guess at a title. "Ms." is safe for women; when in doubt, ask or listen for how a person introduces themselves.

blocks.html: Once you have been introduced, you need to know what to call someone. You learned to use titles with the adults in your life; adults use them with one another, too, especially at first meetings and in writing.
Use a title such as Mr., Ms., Mrs., Mx. or Dr. with the last name until you are invited to use a first name. Always use the name and title a person prefers.

A title is a sign of respect, and starting formal leaves the choice with the other person. Moving from "Ms. Shah" to "Priya" when she invites it is warm; jumping to a first name uninvited can feel presumptuous, especially with older people or at work. Using the name and title a person asks for shows that you listened, which matters more than any rule.

head: Title
Used for
rows: A woman, married or not; the safe choice when you don't know a woman's preference
A married woman who prefers it
A person who prefers a title that does not mark gender
A physician, or anyone with a doctorate who uses the title

blocks.title: A new neighbor
blocks.q: Rosa meets an older neighbor who says, "I'm Walt Hale." What should she call him?
steps: He gave his full name, not an invitation to use "Walt."
She says, "Nice to meet you, Mr. Hale."
If he says, "Please, call me Walt," she happily switches.
blocks.a: "Mr. Hale," until he invites her to use "Walt."

blocks.title: Not sure which title
blocks.q: James is writing to Nora Grant, whom he has never met, and doesn't know whether she uses Ms. or Mrs. What should he write?
steps: "Ms." is correct for any woman, married or not.
If her email signature or reply shows another title, he uses that next time.

blocks.cap: Sort the ways of addressing someone.

blocks.html: Using "Mrs." for any woman who seems married, or guessing at a title. "Ms." is safe for women; when in doubt, ask or listen for how a person introduces themselves. Quick check: did they tell you? Then use exactly that.

Customs differ: in parts of the U.S., "sir" and "ma'am" are everyday courtesy; elsewhere they can sound stiff. Many workplaces use first names from the start. Follow the lead of the person and the place.
